description: Three open pattern-finding scenarios, asked first on 2D maps and then on the 3D table. Facilitator records think-aloud answers. Numbers (rho, n, named areas) are computed by Src/Scripts/build_study_materials.py; nothing here is a measured result.

scenarios.title: Neighbourhood development
scenarios.question: The municipality is choosing neighbourhoods for a targeted development programme and wants to understand how household income and employment relate across the city. Do you see a pattern between them?

a.label: Median income
a.sourceText: SCB Inkomster (Tab11, DeSO): median economic standard per household

b.label: Employment rate, ages 20–64
b.sourceText: SCB Arbetsmarknad (Tab9, DeSO): employed / all residents aged 20–64

scenarios.answer: Areas with higher income also have a higher share of residents in work.
scenarios.planning: Targeted neighbourhood programmes (områdesutveckling) usually pick areas where low income and low employment coincide. This scenario checks whether participants can see that they do.
scenarios.tests: Whether they find a clear relationship, and how fast.

scenarios.title: Preschool and school planning
scenarios.question: The municipality is planning new preschool and school places. A colleague suggests families with children mostly live in the wealthier areas. Look at income and the share of children aged 0–15. Do you agree?

a.label: Median income
a.sourceText: SCB Inkomster (Tab11, DeSO): median economic standard per household

b.label: Share of residents aged 0–15
b.sourceText: SCB Befolkning (Tab1, DeSO): residents 0–15 / all residents

scenarios.answer: Children live in areas at every income level, so school planning has to follow where the children are, not income. The colleague is wrong.
scenarios.planning: A plausible assumption that the data does not support. The colleague's claim raises the bar on purpose: it tests whether the view makes people confirm a pattern they were told to expect.
scenarios.tests: Whether participants report a pattern that is not there (a false positive).
notes: Comes straight after P1, so participants are primed to look for a pattern. That is intended.

scenarios.title: Adult education and SFI
scenarios.question: The municipality is planning adult education and Swedish for immigrants (SFI) and wants to offer courses close to where people live. Is there a pattern between the share of residents born abroad and the share of residents with a higher education?
scenarios.unitLabel: 250 m grid cells with at least 50 residents

a.label: Share of residents born abroad
a.sourceText: SCB Befolkning (Tab4, 250 m grid): residents born abroad / all residents by birth region

b.label: Share with higher education (3+ years), ages 25–64
b.sourceText: SCB Befolkning (Tab10, 250 m grid): post-secondary education of 3 years or more / all education levels, ages 25–64

scenarios.answer: Areas with a higher share of residents born abroad tend to have a lower share of residents with a higher education. The pattern is clear but not perfect: there are exceptions.
scenarios.planning: Adult education and SFI can be offered close to the areas where many residents are born abroad and few have a higher education. The pattern describes areas, not people.
scenarios.tests: A clear but imperfect relationship in opposite directions, on a third kind of area (250 m grid cells) and a new topic (education). Small cells are hidden.
notes: Area pattern only: it says nothing about the education of residents born abroad themselves. Education completed abroad may be missing from SCB's education register, which would make the share look lower (not checked for this delivery).
Only 250 m cells with at least 50 residents are shown; smaller cells and the 1 km cells are 'no data', because shares of a few residents are extreme.

showcase.title: Explore (optional)
showcase.question: If there is time: explore freely. Two things the table can do that a map cannot. Copy: press Copy on the table toolbar (or A on the right controller) and click an area; a 3D copy pops up. Hold the grip with the ray on it to carry it and put it next to another area. Compare: press Compare and click two areas; the Compare panel shows A and B side by side with their differences.
